en: The duty to inform, under the CDC regime, is not satisfied by the mere formal existence of content available to the consumer. In immaterial objects of consumption, information only fulfills its legal function when it organizes, in an intelligible and timely manner, the practical core of the decision. This means that informing is not dumping clauses, FAQs, hyperlinks, peripheral notices and cascading policies only to later invoke formal compliance. Informing is making cognizable, at the point of decision, that which effectively defines the utility of the performance, its risks, its relevant limits, its conditions of enjoyment and its cases of loss. The consumer-law system requires, in material terms, that the supplier ensure the consumer clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product, its economic repercussions and the risks that gravitate around the contracting, so that good faith and trust are not sabotaged by a documentary architecture that delivers words and withholds meaning<1><2>707</2></1>.

<1>p. 619</1> This requirement is especially important in IOCs because the essential content of the relationship is not in peripheral details, but in the very core of the value acquired. Real cost, total cost, mutability of the object, restrictions on use, equivalence parameters, maintenance criteria, cases of loss and consequences of acceptance are not exotic annexes to the contracting. They are the substance of the promised enjoyment. When these elements appear displaced to zones of low visibility, scattered across secondary documents or subordinated to successive cross-references, the duty to inform has not been fulfilled in the material sense, even if the supplier manages to point to dozens of screens, links or supposedly accessible texts. The legal problem ceases to be the simple lack of information and becomes the communicational inadequacy of the supply.

Thus, the key to reading is not quantity, but adequacy. The supplier does not fulfill the legal duty by accumulating documentation and leaving it technically available. Fulfillment is measured by the capacity of the information to reach the consumer under real conditions of guiding a decision. The posture required is not passive. The supplier must make the information reach the recipient in a useful and structured way, because the consumer's right to information is a problem more complex than the mere lack of data to be provided<1><2>708</2></1>. This point is decisive. The standardized defense that “it was all in the terms” only works if one admits, uncritically, that the mere existence of a documentary collection suffices to form valid consent. The CDC does not work with this fiction, so comfortable for the supplier.

From this follows the need to recognize that informational excess can also be a form of violation. Volume is not neutral. In certain communicational designs, it operates as a positive technique of opacity. The information exists, but its organization makes practical understanding of what matters unfeasible. Successive layers of documents, serialized links, cross-references, excessively technical language, inverted visual emphasis, cascading <1>disclaimers</1> and the displacement of relevant content to improbable zones of the contracting flow can produce the same legal effect as omission. The consumer receives text, <2>p. 620</2> but does not receive guidance. The platform stages informational openness while maintaining, under an appearance of compliance, a regime of noise. This is exactly the phenomenon called “performative transparency”.

Performative transparency does not consist in the absence of information, but in the excess, dispersion and defective hierarchization of the essential content. The supplier appears to fulfill the legal duty through abundance, but the communicational design reduces the practical utility of what it presents. This is not a mere aesthetic deficiency of drafting or a discomfort of reading. It is a structure that prevents comparison, understanding of the risk and apprehension of the economic and functional core of the contracting. In a consumer-law key, this failure is legally relevant because it compromises the practical freedom of choice. If the communication reduces price transparency, hinders the comparability of offers and materially interferes with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms, costs and conditions of the product or service, documentary abundance no longer functions as proof of transparency, but as its caricature<1><2>709</2></1>.

This point gains special density in IOCs because enjoyment is usually preceded by purchase and acceptance flows designed for speed, impulse, managed scarcity or a promise of distinction. In such environments, displacing the essential content outside the point of decision is more than a failure of organization. It is a shielding technique. The platform offers the object under a certain frame of value and urgency, but places costs, mutability, potential losses and limitations in documentary zones that the flow itself does not encourage one to go through. The consumer is pushed to decide on the basis of the shop window and only later discovers, if at all, the depth of the contractual reservation against their own enjoyment. The legally relevant question, then, is not whether there was text somewhere in the ecosystem. The question is whether the essential was presented in a conspicuous, legible and timely way before adhesion and before exposure to the risk.

<1>p. 621</1> This is precisely what Article 54, under paragraphs 3 and 4, of the CDC makes explicit. Adhesion contracts must be drafted in clear terms, with conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding, and clauses limiting rights must be drafted with emphasis, allowing immediate and easy understanding<2><3>710</3></2>. The provision is not a typographical whim. It prevents the essential from being hidden in cross-references, low visibility or documentary depth. In IOCs, this command carries even greater weight, because a large part of the relevant limitations falls precisely on the core of the acquired experience. If the platform intends to reserve for itself the power to alter equivalence parameters, reduce functionality, condition the permanence of content, suppress access or redistribute risks, it cannot bury this under textual mountains and then claim that the consumer was informed in advance.

From this perspective, adequate information is that which presents the essential at the moment the consumer needs to decide. Its criterion is neither merely formal nor merely semantic. It is functional. Information must allow use, comparison and concrete evaluation of the performance before adhesion. In practical terms, this means that the informational regime must clearly expose, at the point of decision, the elements that structure the choice: price, total cost, relevant restrictions, ordinary mutability of the object, equivalence criteria, potential loss of items, refund conditions, cases of suspension, limits of use and substantial impacts of updates. When this content is only revealed through later investigation in long documents, consent is already born under a deficit of intelligibility. Adequate information is not that which exists in some remote corner of the system. It is that which arrives in time and with practical utility for deliberation<1><2>711</2></1>.

This shift of focus, from the existence of information to its adequacy, neutralizes the supplier's main alibi in platformized markets. The typical defense maintains that the consumer could have read everything calmly, simply by clicking more, opening more links, following more <1>p. 622</1> cross-references or consulting FAQs and complementary policies. The problem with this defense is that it turns the duty to inform into an obligation of documentary treasure hunting on the part of the consumer. The CDC does not admit this. The protection of trust and good faith prevent the supplier from treating engineered obscurity as proof of contractual freedom. No average consumer can be considered fully informed merely because, in theory, it was possible for them to go through a documentary forest, decode technical vocabulary and reconstruct on their own the hierarchy of what was really essential. When the documentary architecture demands this kind of pilgrimage, transparency has already failed.

For this reason too, excessive cross-references, opaque chains and overly long texts are not legally innocent. The mere mention that certain general conditions exist is not enough to validly include them in the relationship. The consumer must be able to effectively read and understand what the clauses mean, which rights they limit and which obligations they create. Furtive texts, excess of cross-references, dense language and hostile graphic materiality compromise the intelligibility of the essential content and, consequently, the very legitimacy of adhesion<1><2>712</2></1>. Obscurity, here, is not a regrettable stylistic detail. It is a mode of organizing contractual risk for the benefit of the dominant party.

The notion of performative transparency is useful precisely because it captures this difference between formal existence and decisional utility. There is performative transparency when the supplier can demonstrate informational abundance, but cannot demonstrate that the essential core was presented in a clear, conspicuous and functionally guiding way. The performance of compliance replaces the effectiveness of the duty. The system comes to produce proof of formal coverage of the supplier's risk, not of the consumer's enlightenment. On platforms, this is especially visible when purchase screens emphasize urgency, rarity, bonuses, convenience or distinction and reserve the relevant conditions for contractual depth. The contract ceases to be an instrument of information and becomes a piece of ex post shielding.

<1>p. 623</1> The dogmatic consequence is important. If excess, noise and performative transparency can constitute a violation of the duty to inform, legal control cannot be limited to an abstract reading of the contract. It is necessary to reconstruct the concrete form in which the information was displayed, the moment it appeared, the interface that conveyed it, the emphasis it effectively received and the position it occupied in the decision path. In IOCs, proof of informational adequacy depends on minimum documentation of the purchase flow, the confirmation screens, the change notices, the way equivalences are presented and the visual location of the relevant limitations. It is not enough for the platform to claim generically that it informed. It must be in a position to demonstrate how it informed, when it informed and with what emphasis it informed.

It is here that the bridge to auditability is prepared. The transparency required by the CDC, in a governed environment, cannot merely be declared. It must be verifiable. This involves minimum preservation of interface trails, version history of screens, relevant messages, change notices and documentation of the communicational design actually employed. When the proof of this informational regime is concentrated in the supplier, the distribution of the burden cannot remain blind to this asymmetry. Otherwise, the duty to inform becomes a comforting fiction for the platform and an evidentiary nightmare for the consumer. The content of transparency needs to be institutionally reconstructible, or its protection dissolves into formalism.

The objective is to prevent the platform from converting documentary excess into a safe-conduct, dismantling the rhetoric that all available information equals adequate information and putting the duty to inform back on its proper axis, which is that of practical utility for consent, comparison and control. In IOCs, this means shifting the analysis from “the text exists” to “the essential meaning was really placed in conditions to be understood”. The CDC, read functionally, does not protect the supplier who documents too much. It protects the consumer who needs to decide on the basis of what really matters. It is this reading that allows one to move, in the following stages, from the critique of noise to the demand for open auditability and to the reconstruction of enjoyment as a position that cannot be degraded under cover of pseudo-transparency.

The duty to inform, in the CDC system, is not fulfilled by the mere multiplication of texts, links, cross-references, windows, policies and documents formally available to the consumer. Informing, in a material key, means making cognizable in a clear, adequate and conspicuous way the essential content of the consumer relationship, especially that which defines the utility of the performance, its conditions of enjoyment and its relevant risks. This is exactly what is highlighted when interpreting Article 31 of the CDC, affirming that the supplier must ensure the consumer “clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product”, including data related to its characteristics, its economic repercussion, health and safety <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 877)</2>. As a reflection of the principle of transparency, the supplier must offer “clear and correct” information about the qualities of the product and the conditions of the contract, drafting the text clearly, so as to “give the consumer the opportunity” to know the content of the obligations assumed, on pain of the contract not binding them, “even if duly formalized” <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 820-821)</4>. Practices of merely performative transparency, therefore, can constitute a violation of the duty to inform. <5>↩</5>

The duty to inform, in the CDC, is not satisfied by a merely quantitative logic. It is not enough for the supplier to dump documents, links, clauses or textual blocks on the consumer and then claim formal transparency. The legal duty requires positive action oriented toward the effective arrival of the information at its recipient under conditions of relevant understanding. For this reason, “in the regime of consumer relations, the duty to inform the consumer requires an active posture from the supplier”, it being the supplier who “must make the information reach the consumer” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207)</2>. The mere formal provision of content, therefore, is not enough, because there can be documentary access without true cognitive appropriation. The consumer's right to information constitutes “a much more complex question than just a problem of lack of information that needs to be ensured” <3>Wada</3><4>(Beales, Craswell e Salop apud Wada, 2016, p. 82)</4>. The duty to inform, thus, is not fulfilled by volume, by documentary accumulation or by mere formal opening of access, but by informational adequacy. <5>↩</5>

Excess, dispersion, complexity and low hierarchization of the essential characterize forms of functional opacity produced under the appearance of transparency. The starting point lies in the refusal of the simplistic premise according to which it would suffice to add more information to resolve the consumer's informational vulnerability. By recording that the right to information is “a much more complex question than just a problem of lack of information that needs to be ensured” <1>Wada</1><2>(Beales, Craswell e Salop apud Wada, 2016, p. 82)</2>, the logic of mere documentary filling is set aside. This obscurity appears when information is formally provided, but organized in a way that makes comparison and identification of what really matters unfeasible. This is what occurs, for example, in banking packages with numerous products that do not correspond to one another, making it “very difficult for the consumer to compare the benefit packages offered by banks” <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 168-169)</4>. The abusive practice may occur when there is material interference with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms and conditions of the product or service, with an excessive advantage obtained from the lack of understanding of the risks, costs or conditions involved <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 141-142)</6>. In this key, performative transparency is defined precisely by the conspicuous display of content whose form of presentation produces functional opacity. <7>↩</7>

“Paragraph 3. Written adhesion contracts shall be drafted in clear terms and with conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding by the consumer. Paragraph 4. Clauses that imply a limitation of the consumer's rights shall be drafted with emphasis, allowing their immediate and easy understanding.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.. <3>↩</3>

Adequate information, in the consumer-law regime, is not defined by the simple existence of available content, but by its aptitude to present the essential elements of the contracting at the exact moment the consumer needs to decide. For this reason, “information about the performance of the obligation is essential for the consumer” and, “without it, it is not possible to make conscious choices about the product acquired or even about the service contracted” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 206)</2>. This requirement gains density in the prior estimate as a qualified moment of decision, in which the consumer can examine “the quality of the service, the deadline for execution, the materials used”, in short, the essential elements that make up the price and the substance of the performance, being also able to clarify doubts and negotiate the terms before binding themselves <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</4>. Informational adequacy requires organized presentation of the essential content in useful time for deliberation. When the structure of the offer “reduces price transparency”, “the comparability of offers” is hindered <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 168)</6>, which directly compromises the practical freedom of choice. Adequate information, thus, is that which allows one to use and compare the essential before the decision, and not that which merely exists in some remote corner of the contractual ecosystem. <7>↩</7>

The legal sufficiency of information, in the CDC, is not confused with its mere formal availability nor with the existence of a documentary collection potentially consultable by the consumer. Excessive cross-references, opaque chains, overly long texts or a documentary architecture that hinders apprehension of the real content of the obligation do not satisfy the duty to inform in the material sense. No average consumer could understand obligations assumed in contracts that accumulate cross-references to laws and provisional measures in an incomprehensible way, which is why such a bond can be undone for failure of transparency (in this case good faith) at the time of its formation, since the consumer could not understand what obligations they were assuming <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 903)</2>. For the inclusion of general conditions, “the simple mention is not enough” that they will be used; it is necessary that the consumer “be able to read and understand” what the clauses mean, it being frequent that such texts appear in a “somewhat furtive” way, in long or hard-to-read material <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 91-92)</4>. Consequently, documentary excess and formal availability only have legal value if they preserve the material intelligibility of the essential content of the relationship. <5>↩</5>

Advertising, in IOC ecosystems, cannot be treated as a peripheral layer of the offer. It participates directly in the production of the economic meaning of the object, organizes the <1>p. 624</1> consumer's expectation before enjoyment and anticipates, to a large extent, the way in which utility, value, rarity, performance and equivalence will be perceived. It is precisely for this reason that consumer-law protection needs to treat it as a controllable semiotic mechanism. The problem lies not only in literally false sentences or in gross omissions. It lies in the strategic management of the visible and the invisible, of what gains emphasis and what is relegated to the documentary background, of what appears as an immediate advantage and what recedes as a cost, limitation or ordinary risk of the supply.

In platform markets, this question gains special density because the promised experience is not static. The advertised object will later be subjected to updating, curation, parameterization, <1>enforcement</1> and ordinary reconfigurations of the environment. This means that the expectation is not only formed before contracting; it can also be strategically overproduced before the consumer has real conditions to perceive mutability, limits of use, equivalence criteria and ordinary possibilities of functional downgrading. In IOCs, advertising does not announce only an object. It announces a future governed experience. And, for that very reason, it can produce error not only through express falsity, but through the semiotic construction of a trust incompatible with the reality of the regime of enjoyment.

The first point is, then, to recognize advertising as market semiotics. It does not operate only by transferring objective data, but through signs, framings, visual hierarchies and inductions of reading. The relevant vulnerability here is not a lack of technical information in the narrow sense, nor a diffuse psychic weakness of the consumer. What matters is the asymmetry of meaning produced by communication designed to guide adhesion under conditions of selective visibility. The marketing message defines what appears as an advantage, what is naturalized as tolerable, what is anticipated as rarity and what is concealed as an ordinary consequence of the contracting. We are not facing promotional ornament. We are facing a structure for the production of expectation.

This conclusion is perfectly compatible with the dogmatics of the CDC. When advertising contains sufficiently precise elements about qualities, conditions, advantages or characteristics of the object, it becomes part of the offer and radiates obligational effects over the consumer relationship<1><2>713</2></1>. The consumer-law system breaks, therefore, with the old privatist view according to <3>p. 625</3> which advertising would be a simple invitation indifferent to the contracting. In more direct language: the promotional message enters the contract through the door of trust. If the supplier organizes the market through promises, signals and sufficiently guiding descriptions, it cannot later pretend that all of that was only aesthetic ambiance and that the real bond was hidden, dry and hostile, in later clauses. Advertising participates in the very shaping of the legally enforceable performance.

Here, therefore, objective good faith does not appear as a sympathetic abstraction, but as a concrete matrix of ancillary duties in marketing communication. Fair advertising is not merely advertising “without lies”. It is advertising structured in a way compatible with legitimate trust, identification of its persuasive character and consistency between what produces expectation and what will be effectively delivered. Good faith requires that the supplier promise only what it can fulfill and, if it provides information about characteristics of the product, the service or the conditions of contracting, that this information be correct, truthful and apt to guide the formation of will<1><2>714</2></1>. This matters a great deal in IOCs because the formation of expectation usually happens before the consumer has any real contact with the ordinary regime of mutability of the object. The promise circulates first. The frustration comes later.

From this follows the third point: advertising deceptiveness does not depend on a literal lie. The CDC does not require frontal, caricatural or gross falsity to recognize deception. Unlawfulness can arise when the message, even if it contains literally true elements, is apt to lead the consumer into error through ambiguity, relevant omission, strategic incompleteness or <1>p. 626</1> simple persuasive organization of the visible<2><3>715</3></2>. The error need not be fabricated by the openly false sentence. It can be produced by the way the essential is hierarchized, by selective emphasis on advantages and by the displacement of relevant conditions to <4>disclaimers</4>, layers of low visibility, later links or discursive zones that do not usefully integrate the moment of decision.

This is the core of misleading advertising by semiotic architecture. The architecture of the advertisement becomes legally relevant when the supplier structures the consumer's understanding so as to reinforce the positive side of the experience and push the onerous, mutable or limited side out of focus. In simpler terms, communication does not need to lie in order to deceive. It suffices that it manage the interpretive framing in a sufficiently asymmetrical way. Advertising can tell the truth in pieces and still lie as a whole. It can keep the real cost out of the visual center. It can suggest a functional equivalence that the ordinary regime of the IOC later downgrades without verifiable correspondence. It can speak of rarity, urgency, exclusivity or status without adequately integrating, on the same plane of emphasis, the precariousness, reversibility or mutability of what is being acquired.

This mode of operating intensifies when the platform organizes pre-deliveries of expectation. <1>Teasers</1>, shop windows, <2>trailers</2>, event campaigns, passes, rarity panels, countdown timers, suggested equivalences, narratives of distinction and communication through influencers are not merely advance publicity. They are mechanisms of curation of expectation prior to effective enjoyment. In IOCs, this is of enormous relevance because the governance of the decision begins before the purchase and before acceptance. The platform constructs in advance what the consumer expects to find, value, fear losing and tolerate as admissible frustration. The marketing environment, thus, already functions as an architecture of the future tolerable disappointment. If the expectation is inflated by a semiotics of value and later absorbed <3>p. 627</3> by an ordinary regime of downgrading, elastic equivalence or unilateral mutability, advertising was not merely a pre-contractual stage. It was a mechanism for capturing trust.

In this context, the case of hybrid formats is especially important. In digital ecosystems, advertising, content, entertainment, recommendation and sale are frequently confused. Influencers, creators, “community” posts, demonstrative experiences, in-game shop windows and events mediated by the platform's own environment make less sharp the distinction between descriptive communication, cultural recommendation and marketing persuasion. This hybridization weakens the intelligibility of the advertising character of the message and compromises communicational fairness. The consumer need not be facing a banner explicitly labeled as an advertisement to be persuasively guided toward a contracting. When identification of the marketing character is weakened, the semiotic asymmetry deepens, because advertising ceases to be perceived as advertising and comes to operate disguised as experience, recommendation or simple ecosystem content.

It is precisely for this reason that Article 38 of the CDC proves so important here. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it<1><2>716</2></1>. This is not an elegant evidentiary detail. It is a normative recognition that advertising is a space of power and, therefore, of responsibility. In IOCs, this provision prevents the consumer from having to prove alone that the expectation produced by the communication was incompatible with the effective regime of enjoyment. If the platform announces a certain equivalence, a certain benefit, a certain utility, a certain standard of stability or a certain implicit value of rarity, it is for the platform to demonstrate documentarily the correctness of this narrative in light of what is ordinarily delivered and administered in the ecosystem. The system does not presume the innocence of the marketing promise. It requires that it be sustained by whoever produced it.

This logic is very strongly articulated with the protection of trust. Legally protected trust is born not only from the final contractual instrument, but also from the communicational behavior of the supplier in the market<1><2>717</2></1>. The more precise, eloquent <3>p. 628</3> and guiding the advertising, the greater its aptitude to generate legitimate expectation and, therefore, the greater also its binding force. This is decisive because it prevents the old maneuver of capturing trust in the pre-contractual phase and then trying to dehydrate it in the final text of the contract or in mutable internal rules. Advertising does not stay outside, since it participates in the legally relevant core of the consumer relationship. If it organizes the expectation, it also organizes the parameter by which the frustration will be measured.

The discipline of children's advertising functions, here, as a normative limit case that internally reinforces this reading without diverting the axis of the discussion. The point is not to equate adults with children, nor to open a new thematic front. The point is to show that the CDC itself already recognizes that abusiveness can result from taking advantage of a structural deficiency of judgment exploited by persuasive communication. When the system considers abusive the advertising that takes advantage of the child's deficiency of judgment and experience, it recognizes, in an explicit key, that the manipulation of meaning and the exploitation of limitations of decoding are legally relevant. The most important normative datum is not childhood in itself, but the underlying logic. When communication takes advantage of a structural asymmetry of understanding, the control of abusiveness intensifies. This reinforces, from within the system itself, the legitimacy of treating semiotic vulnerability as a legal fact and not as a sociological metaphor.

The argumentative utility of this limit case is quite elegant. It shows that the CDC already operates with gradations of vulnerability linked to real conditions of understanding and resistance, and not only to the episodic lack of data. Advertising can be abusive even without lying, simply because it exploits a structural limitation of judgment. Transposing this reasoning in a controlled way to IOCs, without infantilizing the adult consumer, it is maintained that there are also situations in which architecture, curation and private governance of meaning produce real asymmetries of decoding, comparison and proof. When these asymmetries are systematically exploited by advertising and by the communicational environment of the platform, space opens for reinforced control of deceptiveness and abusiveness.

The immediate dogmatic consequence is that advertising in IOCs must be treated as a controllable practice when the essential is kept out of focus and the negative is displaced to <1>p. 629</1> <2>disclaimers</2> or useless cross-references; when marketing communication produces, through anticipatory curation of expectation, an image of value, rarity, performance or functional equivalence that the ordinary regime of mutability later frustrates without verifiable correspondence; and when the marketing character of the message is weakened by hybrid formats that confuse content, recommendation, entertainment and sale. In these cases, deceptiveness is not reduced to a literal lie. It appears as a defect of the very architecture of the promise.

It is necessary, then, to connect semiotic vulnerability, good faith, trust, deceptiveness and abusiveness without psychologizing consumption or resorting to moralism against advertising in itself. The problem is not desiring, fantasizing or attributing symbolic value to the object. The problem is when the marketing production of expectation is organized so as to guide the consumer's understanding toward an image of the object that the supply regime itself does not sustain, or sustains only under hidden reservations, opaque equivalences and silent mutability. Advertising thus ceases to be merely an announcement and becomes an objective element in the production of a legally controllable trust.

With this, the transition is then prepared to the broader decision environment in which advertising, information, interface and choice architecture operate in an integrated way. Advertising will not be the only gear of semiotic vulnerability, but it is one of its most powerful cores. It pre-shapes expectation, organizes the imaginary of value, distributes visibility and conditions what the consumer understands as risk, opportunity and loss. In IOCs, where enjoyment is governed and mutable, this makes it one of the main points of control of the CDC. The supplier answers not only for what it promises in isolated sentences. It answers for the regime of meaning it produces when it advertises.

Under the regime of the Consumer Protection Code, advertising does not occupy a merely peripheral or ornamental position. When the advertising message contains sufficiently precise elements about the object, its qualities, conditions or advantages, it becomes part of the offer and comes to radiate obligational effects over the consumer relationship, binding the supplier to the content conveyed <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 140-142)</2>. The consequence is direct: advertising does not remain outside the contract as a simple prior persuasive stage, but participates in the shaping of the legally enforceable content of the performance. This logic is reinforced by the overcoming of the old privatist understanding that treated advertising as a simple harmless invitation to contract. In the consumer-law system, the marketing message ceases to be legally indifferent and comes to function as a source of obligation whenever, by its degree of precision and aptitude to form expectation, it makes up the content of the offer addressed to the consumer <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 144)</4>. If advertising is part of the offer and produces obligational binding, then the way in which it organizes the consumer's understanding, hierarchizes elements, distributes visibility and produces expectation also becomes legally relevant. The advertising message does not stay outside the relationship doing marketing; it participates in the very obligational structure of the supply. <5>↩</5>

Marketing communication, under the CDC regime, is subject to material control of fairness, truthfulness and adequacy because it is capable of shaping the consumer's legitimate expectation even before the bond is formalized. Marques states that, in matters of advertising, objective good faith requires it to be “a fair activity”, reflected also from the position of whoever receives the message, such that it promises only what it can fulfill and, if it brings information about characteristics of the product, the service or the contractual conditions, that these be correct and truthful <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 832; p. 886)</2>. The author adds that the main characteristic of misleading advertising, according to the CDC, is being liable to lead the consumer into error, including by “omissions”, the rule having to be interpreted broadly, since the error consists in a “false notion of reality” potentially formed in the consumer's mind by the advertising action <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 909)</4>. Applied to the problem of semiotic architecture, this guideline authorizes control of promotional messages that, without lying frontally, organize the interpretive field of the offer so as to produce an illusory understanding of utility, extent, stability or conditions of enjoyment. <5>↩</5>

Advertising deceptiveness, in the CDC, does not depend on literal falsity or on a frontally demonstrable lie. Unlawfulness can arise whenever the message, even if partially true, is apt to lead the consumer into error, including through omission, ambiguity, relevant incompleteness or the very form of presentation of the content <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 167)</2>. The decisive point is not the microscopic truthfulness of each isolated sentence, but the deceptive potential of the meaningful whole of the communication as effectively perceived by its recipient. This perception becomes especially important when the essential datum is displaced to zones of low visibility, diluted in accessory information or weakened by graphic and drafting strategies that reduce its practical apprehension. Deceptiveness can emerge, for example, when the real price does not appear clearly, when charges are relegated to a visually irrelevant position or when the decisive information is technically included, but functionally hidden in the context of the piece <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 168)</4>. Misleading advertising by semiotic architecture does not require gross falsity. It can operate through the strategic management of the visible and the invisible, through the functional ambiguity of language and through the persuasive organization of the advertisement so as to guide the consumer's understanding away from what really matters. <5>↩</5>
“Art. 38. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.. <3>↩</3>

Advertising, in consumer law, participates directly in the formation of contractual trust. This occurs because, in markets marked by lean, opaque or gap-ridden adhesion contracts, the marketing message frequently anticipates, completes and densifies the understanding that the consumer forms about the utility, the qualities and the mode of enjoyment of the object offered, becoming a relevant element for the construction of their legitimate expectation <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 142)</2>. Legally protected trust is not born, therefore, only from the final contractual instrument, but also from the communicational behavior of the supplier in the market. This binding can be understood in light of the protection of the expectation provoked by the advertiser's own conduct. The more eloquent, precise and guiding the message, the greater its aptitude to generate trust worthy of protection and, therefore, the greater also its binding force <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 42)</4>. Advertising not only describes the object, but pre-shapes the expectation of enjoyment that will later serve as the parameter for assessing performance, inadequacy and deceptiveness. When marketing communication structures the consumer's expectation, it enters the legally relevant core of the consumer relationship and can be a source both of obligation and of legally censurable frustration. <5>↩</5>

Semiotic vulnerability, in order to have dogmatic utility, cannot be treated as a loose cultural metaphor nor as a judgment about the consumer's psychology. It designates a <1>p. 580</1> contemporary form of factual vulnerability produced by the way supply is organized in platform environments. In IOCs, the relevant asymmetry does not reside only in the fact that the consumer knows less about the internal characteristics of the system. It arises because the platform controls the very instruments of intelligibility of the relationship, that is, the signs, interfaces, metrics, framings and records through which the consumer forms expectation, assesses enjoyment, perceives downgrading and tries to sustain a challenge. The consumer's vulnerability remains the pillar of the special protection of the CDC, and it is precisely for this reason that semiotic vulnerability must be understood as a contemporary specification of this structural datum, and not as a parallel or extravagant category <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 324; p. 307)</3><4><5>650</5></4>.

This point requires an important distinction. Semiotic vulnerability does not describe lesser individual discernment, psychological naivety or subjective susceptibility of the user. The problem lies in the objective way in which the environment organizes language, visibility, comparison and proof. On platforms, the consumer depends on governed mediations to understand what they acquired, perceive whether the experience was altered and identify whether there was a legally relevant loss. This means that the platform not only supplies the object, but also administers the references through which this object can be perceived and measured. The asymmetry, then, ceases to be merely informational in the classical sense and becomes also semiotic, because the supplier controls the regime of production of meaning of enjoyment itself.

It is precisely this that sustains the category under the CDC. The consumer's vulnerability does not act only as the sociological background of the system. It is normatively articulated with good faith, the duty to inform, transparency and the protection of trust. The consumer's autonomy depends on positive duties to inform, cooperate, act with fairness and care, because without this minimum level of conduct the decision to contract does not come to be rational in a <1>p. 581</1> legally relevant sense <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 812; p. 1480)</3><4><5>651</5></4>. Semiotic vulnerability is anchored exactly in this gearing. It shows that, in governed environments, the duty to inform cannot be reduced to a bureaucratic dumping of data nor to rituals of acceptance. What is at stake is the production of minimum conditions for effective understanding of enjoyment and of its relevant alterations.

For this reason, informational inadequacy is not limited to pure and simple omission. The supplier can appear transparent and, even so, produce material opacity through excess, dispersion, low practical utility, excessively technical language or communicational organization that frustrates understanding. It is not enough to ensure formal access to information. It must be correct, clear, precise and conspicuous, without useless prolixity or strategic scarcity, and the supplier cannot structure barriers that interfere negatively with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms and conditions of the contracting <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207; p. 142)</2><3><4>652</4></3>. Again, this allows semiotic vulnerability to be formulated without psychologizing the consumer. The problem is not inner weakness. The problem is a communicational architecture that appears to inform while organizing noise.

From this follows a decisive consequence: in IOCs, the platform controls not only the modulation of the object. It also controls the means by which the modulation can be perceived, named and compared. Shop windows, metrics, rarities, narratives of prestige, <1>p. 582</1> reputational systems, visual <2>feedbacks</2>, progression histories and interface framings cease to be peripheral elements of the environment and come to make up the intelligibility of the consumed object itself. When these elements are reorganized unilaterally, the relevant loss can be obscured under an appearance of continuity. The consumer keeps nominal access, but loses functional or symbolic utility without finding clear criteria to measure the erosion. It is this type of asymmetry that the category seeks to make visible.

The CDC already offers instruments for this because the problem is not limited to the abstract plane of communication. Abusive practices involve precisely taking advantage of the supplier's position of power to impose behaviors on the consumer in violation of the duties of fairness, collaboration and respect for legitimate expectations. Abusiveness can also arise from the asymmetrical exploitation of the relevant meanings of the consumer relationship, especially when extensive, obscure or surprising clauses compromise the quality of the information and the consent of the adhering party <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 328-329; p. 388)</2><3><4>653</4></3>. Semiotic vulnerability remains, thus, in the trunk of consumer law. It merely names with more precision a current form of exploitation of vulnerability already intuited by the institutes of the system.

This reading also clarifies why the “governed environment” does not compete with the “immaterial product”. In the IOC regime, the governed environment is a condition of legal existence of the consumed product itself. The object is only enjoyable while the platform maintains, administers and modulates access, signs, rules of use and parameters of intelligibility. This means that the environment does not figure as an external frame of the performance, but as a constitutive element of the product as legally consumed. Relevant alterations in the architecture of enjoyment can correspond, in dogmatic terms, to alterations of the object of consumption itself. <1>p. 583</1> Semiotic vulnerability makes intelligible precisely the asymmetry generated by this arrangement, because the platform simultaneously administers the object and the means of reading the object.

This category also reorganizes classic problems of the CDC. If enjoyment depends on continuous maintenance and modulation, delivery cannot be thought of as a pure one-off act. If utility is reconfigurable, inadequacy is not limited to the ostensible defect of a static thing. If there is no sharp final milestone of execution, the identification of the quality defect needs to dialogue with the real moment in which the degradation becomes perceptible and verifiable. If the promise circulates through signs, advertising, narratives and interfaces, the correspondence between offer and enjoyment cannot be measured only by the literalness of a contractual text. Semiotic vulnerability functions, then, as a category of attribution of the structural asymmetry that justifies reconstructing the duty to inform, trust, adequacy and abusiveness in an opaque and mutable environment.

This problem directly reaches the plane of proof. In technically sophisticated ecosystems, the supplier controls not only the service, but also the documents, the records, the technique and the very intelligibility of the relationship. Often, the consumer's difficulty is not only economic, but factual and technical. The necessary evidence is not in their power. It is with whoever administers the environment, the <1>logs</1>, the parameterizations and the relevant histories.

Facilitating the defense and redistributing the burden of proof become decisive in relationships of this nature. The technological specialization of the service and the dominant position of the supplier make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only instrument capable of effectively enabling the protection of the consumer <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 854; p. 283)</2><3><4>654</4></3>. Semiotic vulnerability is, at this point, also evidentiary vulnerability.

The protection of the consumer, then, is not satisfied with formally available information. It requires informed and conscious contracting to a sufficient degree for the consumer to be able to know, decide and use the product or service adequately. The information <1>p. 584</1> protected by the system is worth its practical utility in compensating vulnerability, and not as a bureaucratic ritual of unloading data <2>Wada</2><3>(Wada, 2016, p. 211; p. 143)</3><4><5>655</5></4>. On platforms, this means that intelligibility is not communicational ornament. It is a functional presupposition of the very decisional utility of information and, therefore, of the legitimacy of the supply.

The foundational basis of the dogmatic utility of the category is thus identified. Semiotic vulnerability does not replace the <1>standards</1> formulated nor is it confused with them. It identifies the relevant structural asymmetry in IOCs and allows the problem to be brought back to classic categories of the CDC without reducing the controversy to a “mere environmental problem” external to the object. From it, the following steps of the argument become manageable, in particular the requirement of institutional verifiability, the reconstruction of adequacy in a key of functional integrity and a more realistic distribution of the burden of proof in the face of opaque and governed mutations of enjoyment.

The formulation of semiotic vulnerability, in order to remain dogmatically useful, must be understood as a contemporary development of a structural datum that already organizes the consumer-law microsystem: the consumer's vulnerability as the permanent foundation of the protective interpretation of the CDC. It is not a matter of creating a parallel category, disconnected from the grammar of the system, but of specifying, in the context of platforms, one of the ways in which the imbalance of forces between supplier and consumer manifests itself today. Marques states this quite directly in affirming that, in consumer contracts, "the problem is the flagrant imbalance of forces of the contracting parties. One of the parties is vulnerable (art. 4º. I), it is the weakest pole of the contractual relationship, since it cannot discuss the content of the contract", being left, as a rule, only to accept or reject the predisposed package <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 324)</2>. The author adds that the definition of consumer constitutes "the pillar that sustains the special protection", because this exists only by reason of the vulnerability of the consumer party in market relations <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 307)</4>. Semiotic vulnerability, in this key, appears as a contemporary form of factual vulnerability, traceable to good faith, the duty to inform, the protection of trust and contractual balance. <5>↩</5>

The consumer's vulnerability, in the CDC, does not act only as a sociological premise of the protective regime; it is normatively articulated with objective good faith and with the duty to inform, forming an operative core for containing the typical asymmetries of the market. This means that the structural fragility of the consumer is legally confronted through the imposition of positive duties on the supplier, above all at the level of the formation and conduct of the contractual relationship. Marques makes this gearing explicit in highlighting that the idea of "rational autonomy" depends precisely on the incidence of ancillary duties to inform, cooperate, treat the consumer with fairness and care, since only with this "new level of conduct in the market" can one achieve a "truly reflected, autonomous and 'rational" will of the consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812)</2>. In a convergent sense, the author states that the CDC seeks "transparency and harmony in consumer relations", imposing good faith as a requirement to prevent market practices from "making use of the vulnerability of consumers", the duty to inform being "a basic duty of suppliers" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1480)</4>. This keeps semiotic vulnerability anchored in the normative ground of the microsystem. <5>↩</5>

In this sense, Wada (20216) allows one to show that informational inadequacy, in consumer law, is not reduced to the pure and simple absence of data. The failure can also arise when the supplier ensures only formal access to information, but does so under conditions that frustrate its practical intelligibility. The problem, then, is not only omitting, but communicating in a materially insufficient way, through excess, dispersion, complexity or low concrete utility. Along these lines, the author expressly states that “it is not enough to ensure formal access to information”, it being necessary that it have the legally required attributes of “correctness, clarity, precision and conspicuousness” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207)</2>. The requirement is qualitative, not merely quantitative. This key allows one to understand that informational noise also makes vulnerable. Information must be “precise (= not prolix or scarce)”, precisely so that it remains comprehensible and functional to the consumer's decision process <3>Wada</3><4>(Marques apud Wada, 2016, p. 207)</4>. Furthermore, the author observes that the supplier cannot interfere “significantly and negatively with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms or conditions” of the contracting, nor establish “barriers or difficulties” to understanding <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 142)</6>. Hence the pertinence of treating semiotic vulnerability as a contemporary form of factual vulnerability: not because the consumer is psychologically weak, but because they can be exposed to communicational architectures that appear transparent while producing material opacity. <7>↩</7>

The formulation of semiotic vulnerability remains internal to the CDC when it is read from the articulation between vulnerability, good faith, the duty to inform, trust and abusive practices. Abusive practices involve a violation of the supplier's duty of fairness toward the consumer, standing out, in many cases, the exploitation of the supplier's position and power to impose a certain behavior on the consumer. In these cases, there is a violation of the duties of fairness, collaboration and respect for legitimate expectations arising from objective good faith, which includes positive duties of clarification and transparent counseling, as well as a duty to abstain from conduct that takes advantage of vulnerability and affects the consumer's freedom to negotiate <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 328-329)</2>. This key is reinforced in the treatment of surprise clauses. Their abusiveness results, even before the breach of balance in the strict sense, from the violation of the duty to inform the consumer, above all in overly extensive or complex contracts entered into by a lay consumer. In these situations, the supplier is bound by a duty of adequate clarification, on pain of informational insufficiency being presumed and the quality of consent being compromised <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 388)</4>. The category of semiotic vulnerability, thus, does not abandon the trunk of consumer law; it merely names, with more precision, a contemporary form of factual vulnerability already intuited by its own institutes: the asymmetrical exploitation of the relevant meanings of the consumer relationship. <5>↩</5>

The CDC's response to contemporary asymmetries is not limited to the material plane of information and abusiveness; it already reaches the procedural plane of proof as well. The specialization and technological sophistication of products and services, added to the consumer's economic or technical weakness, make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only resource apt to make the claim succeed. This is explained by the dominant position of the supplier, which holds in-depth technical knowledge and controls documents, records and the contracting process itself <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 854)</2>. Often, the consumer's impossibility of demonstrating their reasons results from the simple fact that the necessary evidence is not in their power, but with the supplier. This is not only an economic obstacle, but a factual impossibility linked to the absence of conditions, including technical ones, for producing evidence, because the power of direction and specialized knowledge belong, as a rule, to the supplier <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 283)</4>. Semiotic vulnerability, in this key, can also be perceived as a contemporary form of evidentiary vulnerability: whoever controls not only the service, but the records, the technique and the intelligibility of the relationship, also controls a good part of the conditions for challenging it. The CDC already reacts to this by redistributing burdens and facilitating the defense. <5>↩</5>

The protection of the consumer is directly linked to the requirement of information that is not merely formally available, but materially apt to guide a decision. Legally adequate communication needs to produce effectively informed and conscious contracting, that is, a state of understanding sufficient for the consumer to know what they are binding themselves to and to be able to deliberate in a minimally autonomous way. For this reason, Wada states that, for the normative program of protection against abusive commercial practices, it is essential to ensure the consumer “an informed and conscious contracting”, since “only thus will they be able to make their decision and assume the commitment with the supplier” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</2>. This requirement has a clearly rebalancing function. The information protected by the consumer-law system is not worth anything in itself, as a bureaucratic rite of unloading data, but for its practical utility in compensating the consumer's vulnerability. The author observes that this limit imposed on the supplier seeks precisely to “rebalance the consumer relationship”, providing the consumer with the opportunity to “know, negotiate and decide” <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</4>. In a convergent sense, the author maintains that, given the consumer's lack of capacity to choose or use the product or service adequately, the supplier has the duty to provide the performance under conditions that allow the consumer to “make their choices and use the product or service adequately” <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 143)</6>. Intelligibility, thus, is not communicational adornment: it is a functional presupposition of the decisional utility of information. <7>↩</7>

In platform contexts, information, advertising and abusive practices cannot be examined as autonomous phenomena, isolated in watertight compartments, because, in the real process of consumption, they operate jointly in the formation of expectation, urgency, trust and tolerance to frustration. The legal problem is no longer exhausted in knowing whether a given clause existed, whether certain information was technically available or whether an advertising piece contained literal falsity. What needs to be controlled is the integrated decision arrangement through which the platform organizes the consumer's adhesion to and permanence in the <1>p. 630</1> ecosystem, distributing visibility, scarcity, comparability and promise of value in a way functional to its own interests. In IOCs, this becomes even more sensitive because the consumed object does not stabilize as a thing delivered once and for all. The consumer's decision falls on a future governed experience, continuously modulated by architecture, curation and <2>enforcement</2>, so that the initial expectation comes to make up the very legal substance of enjoyment.

This finding requires an important methodological shift. Information cannot be read only as declaratory content; advertising cannot be treated as promotional ornament; and the abusive practice cannot be reduced to a marginal event subsequent to the contract. What exists, in many cases, is a single communicational and decisional environment in which promise, selective visibility, managed scarcity, symbolic rewards, choice architecture and rituals of acceptance act together to produce adhesion. Transparency, in this frame, is not a mere formal requirement of the final instant of contracting, but a presupposition that must run through the entire process of the consumer's approach to the object, from the capture of their attention to the settling of their expectation as to what will be obtained, lost or tolerated as admissible frustration<1><2>718</2></1>. For this reason, the legality of the relationship cannot be assessed only by the final text of the bond, but by the set of pre-contractual and contextual manifestations that shaped the will and the consumer's perception of risk.

It is precisely in this framework that hypercuratorial anticipation gains dogmatic relevance. The platform does not administer only the present experience of enjoyment. It administers, before it, the very horizon of expectation on the basis of which the consumer decides. Temporary events, selected shop windows, curated rarity, artificial urgency, promises of distinction, teaserization of utility, suggested equivalences and cycles of emotional intensification make up a grammar of anticipation that acts on the way the consumer learns to desire, to hope and to fear loss. The environment comes to govern not only access to the object, but the future interpretation of the value of this object. This <1>p. 631</1> profoundly alters the reading of information, advertising and abusiveness, because the promise is no longer a lateral phenomenon. It becomes a structural component of the regime of governed enjoyment.

In these contexts, the platform produces something more sophisticated than simple ordinary commercial persuasion. It builds cycles of promise, intensification and partial delivery, in which the object is presented as a rare, prestigious, limited or virtually guaranteed opportunity, even though effective enjoyment depends on later mechanisms of randomness, mutability, internal rebalancing or unilaterally defined equivalences. The consumer is induced to adhere not only by a stated advantage, but by an architecture of expectation that teaches them to read that acquisition as a decisive moment, an imminent loss or a singular chance. The decision, thus, is formed within an environment that administers in advance the meaning of value. And it is precisely there that relevant omission, misleading advertising and abusiveness can arise in an articulated way, with no need for a frontal lie or for a complete absence of information.

Relevant omission appears when the essential is deliberately displaced out of the decisional focus. The supplier emphasizes urgency, benefit, rarity or prestige, but relegates to lateral conditions what really defines the substance of enjoyment, such as relevant limitations of use, ordinary mutability of the object, equivalence parameters, possible losses, restricted windows of use, additional requirements for the promise to materialize or specific conditions for maintaining the advertised value. Misleading advertising, in turn, manifests itself when the image of utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in the effective experience of enjoyment, either because the platform later downgrades the object, or because the initial promise already concealed, through ambiguity or an architecture of visibility, the real way in which utility would be delivered. Abusive advertising, finally, appears when the design of the environment systematically exploits the consumer's vulnerability, compressing their space for deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward, ritualization of acceptance and fragmentation of the relevant conditions.

This reading prevents two symmetrical errors. The first would be to moralize every technique of commercial persuasion, as if all intense advertising, all interface curation or all architecture aimed at conversion were, in itself, unlawful. That is not it. The market can promote, persuade, dramatize and organize interest. What the CDC does not admit is that this organization of interest operate through functional opacity, capture of expectation and displacement of the essential out of the useful field of understanding. The second error would be to imagine that there is only a problem when the advertising piece, in isolation, contains literal falsity or when a certain <1>p. 632</1> clause, in isolation, is abusive. In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, unlawfulness can reside precisely in the articulation between elements that, seen separately, seem neutral, but that, combined, govern the consumer's decision in a structurally asymmetrical way.

At this point, the role of advertising needs to be brought back to its correct dogmatic place. It is not external to the contract, nor simple cultural ambiance of the market. Marketing communication actively participates in manufacturing the disposition to contract, inflating needs, organizing desires and simultaneously presenting the path to their satisfaction<1><2>719</2></1>. Instead of a clean and compartmentalized sequence between advertisement, information and contracting, what exists is a communicational continuum in which the platform produces expectation, guides the reading of the object, administers the rhythm of the decision and only then stabilizes acceptance in documentary forms that frequently do not reflect, with the same emphasis, the promise that triggered the bond. This means that abusiveness cannot be located only in the final statement, because the pre-contractual environment itself already participates in the material constitution of consent.

This conclusion is reinforced when one observes that, on platforms, marketing communication frequently dissolves into hybrid formats. Recommendation, entertainment, tutorial, community narrative, demonstration of use, influencer content and advertising piece are confused, reducing the consumer's critical vigilance and scrambling the perception of the persuasive status of the message. In these cases, the legal problem lies not only in the content communicated, but in the very way it is inserted into the decision flow, diminishing the intelligibility that it is a commercial push and maximizing its aptitude to produce adhesion<1><2>720</2></1>. The abusive arrangement, then, does not depend on an <3>p. 633</3> explicit banner or a classic advertisement. It may reside precisely in this dissolution of advertising into the environment, which makes it more effective as a technique for steering behavior and more opaque as a source of obligation and control.

This has direct consequences for the relationship between information, advertising and abusive practices. In IOCs, the supplier does not merely transmit messages about a previously given object. It administers signs and metrics that constitute the very perceived value of enjoyment. Advertising does not surround the object externally; it helps produce it as an expectation of performance, distinction, utility or permanence. Information does not serve only to describe this object; it defines to what extent the consumer can understand its real conditions of use and its ordinary margins of alteration. And the abusive practice does not appear only when there is brutal imposition or a scandalous clause; it can emerge from a decision ecosystem in which urgency, scarcity, performative transparency and elastic equivalences work together to induce adhesion in a context of materially defective understanding.

The duty to inform, in this context, can no longer be conceived as an obligation of textual deposit. When the platform operates under hypercuratorial anticipation, informing comes to mean making reconstructible, at the exact moment of decision, that which the anticipatory curation itself tries to obscure. It is not enough for text to exist. The essential content must be presented in a comparable, hierarchized, conspicuous and timely way. If the promotional architecture of the environment creates intensity and scarcity to hasten the decision, the duty to inform needs to function as a counterweight to this acceleration, and not as a bureaucratic ritual consummated in background documents. Likewise, advertising cannot be evaluated only by its microscopic statement, because its aptitude to deceive or abuse also depends on how it is inserted in the flow, what it highlights, what it omits, what equivalences it suggests and the way it administers the perception of time, risk and loss.

The most important methodological consequence of the item is this: consumer-law analysis must consider the whole of the communicational and decisional arrangement, and not only isolated fragments of its formal expression. The jurist needs to ask how the expectation was produced, at what moment the relevant conditions were revealed, with what emphasis they appeared, what was the effective sequence between promise and acceptance, and whether the consumer had real means to <1>p. 634</1> understand and compare what was offered to them. This places choice architecture back within the field of the CDC without technological mysticism and without creating a parallel law of platforms. It is merely a matter of recognizing that, when information, advertising and design operate together to govern the decision, legal control also needs to reach them in an integrated way<2><3>721</3></2>.

With this shift, two operators are prepared. The first is open auditability, because, if abusiveness can reside in the communicational regime of the supply, it is necessary that this regime be institutionally reconstructible, with minimum preservation of screens, flows, messages, promotional pieces, interface alterations and decision trails. The second is functional value equivalence, because the expectation produced by hypercuratorial anticipation cannot be discarded as promotional smoke when it served precisely to induce the acquisition and shape the understanding of the object. If the platform promises a curated experience of value, rarity, performance or advantage, and later rebalances or downgrades it under opaque criteria, the frustration is not a mere annoyance. It may be a relevant inadequacy of the governed enjoyment itself.

In contexts under hypercuratorial anticipation, information, advertising and abusive practices belong to the same dogmatic problem. The platform does not merely offer an object; it organizes the semiotic field in which this object will be desired, understood and accepted. It is in this field that the consumer learns what counts as an advantage, what losses they should fear, what costs they can ignore and what frustrations they should bear as normal. When this organization of meaning is conducted so as to displace the essential, manipulate expectation and induce tolerance to loss under an appearance of freedom of choice, the CDC is not facing peripheral details of the digital experience. It is facing the very contemporary mode of exploitation of vulnerability in IOCs.

The consumer-law discipline of the decision environment does not authorize artificially separating information, advertising and the formation of will as if each of these dimensions operated in an isolated compartment. In the real process of consumption, especially in contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, these elements act in an integrated way to shape the consumer's expectation, urgency, trust and practical disposition to adhere to and remain in the bond. The meaning of the transparency mandate can be traced back to the search for the “true and free will of the consumer”, functioning as a “precondition” for them to freely express their will and realize their legitimate expectations, that is, those that led them, “duly informed about the product or service, aware of their future contractual rights and duties”, to choose a certain supplier as a contractual partner <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 818-819)</2>. This shows that transparency is not limited to the final instant of acceptance, but must characterize every pre-contractual manifestation of the supplier in the market. <3>↩</3>

Advertising and offer, in the consumer market, do not operate as watertight acts. Marketing communication participates in manufacturing the very disposition to contract by inflating needs, organizing desires and simultaneously presenting the path to their satisfaction, leading the consumer to the culminating moment of adhesion <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 91])</2>. For this reason, the legal reading of the decision process cannot artificially separate, into autonomous compartments, advertising, information and contracting, as if each of these layers acted in isolation. This inseparability is accentuated because the marketing message usually brings together, in a single arrangement, concrete offers, fanciful promises and accessory advantages integrated into a marketing mix, in such a way that the social action of advertisers becomes a source of duties and obligations <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 95])</4>. In contexts under hypercuratorial anticipation, abusiveness is not located only in an isolated statement, but may emerge from the communicational regime of the supply as a whole, that is, from the integrated way in which offer, persuasion and management of expectation are articulated to steer the consumer's decision. <5>↩</5>

Communicational unlawfulness, in the CDC, is not restricted to frontal, conspicuous advertising easily identifiable as such. It can also arise in hybrid, disguised arrangements or ones incorporated into apparently neutral media, in which the commercial message infiltrates narrative contexts that reduce the consumer's critical vigilance and intensify their vulnerability to inducement <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 123-125])</2>. This occurs when marketing communication presents itself as entertainment, reporting or neutral recommendation, although it functions, in practice, as a vector of commercial steering, which is why the responsibility of the outlet lies precisely in not allowing confusion between advertising and editorial matter <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 123-125])</4>. The legal problem, in these cases, lies not only in the content conveyed, but in the very scrambling of the status of the message. In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, abusiveness may result from the entire regime of inducement, and not only from a classic advertising piece, above all when commercial communication dissolves into hybrid formats that confuse the consumer about the nature of what they see, read or follow. <5>↩</5>

The legal analysis of contractual and communicational mechanisms that affect the consumer's decision cannot be compartmentalized without a serious loss of adherence to the reality of the bond. Under the CDC regime, the consumer contract is not reduced to the final text of the predisposed clauses, because the consumer's will is formed throughout a relational process in which advertising, information provided, commercial practices, accessory promises and inducement techniques materially participate in building expectation and adhesion. The interpreter of the consumer contract must observe not only the rule of Article 47 of the CDC, but all the rules of the Code that establish rights and duties of consumer and supplier, so that “the content of the contract to be interpreted is not only that ‘placed’ in clauses pre-drafted unilaterally by the supplier, but also the entire prior context that constitutes the offer”, such as advertising, brochures, information and commercial practices <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1015)</2>. This contextual interpretation seeks the meaning of the contract also in its negotiating context, considering prior acts and information as legally relevant and forming the whole to be considered <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1030)</4>. Consequently, in environments under hypercuratorial anticipation, Consumer Law must examine together the mechanisms of information, advertising and choice architecture, since it is precisely from this integrated operation that the capture of expectation, the management of urgency and the exploitation of vulnerability may emerge. <5>↩</5>
